questions.q: What distinguishes a planning agent from a purely reactive agent?
options: A planning agent decomposes the goal into an ordered sequence of steps upfront (or periodically), rather than deciding only the single immediate next action
A planning agent can never call more than one tool in its entire run
A planning agent has no ability to revise its approach once started
A planning agent and a reactive agent are functionally identical
questions.explain: Reactive agents pick the next single action based only on current state; planning agents lay out a multi-step plan toward the goal, revising it as needed.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does an upfront plan matter if it can be revised mid-execution anyway?
options: It doesn't matter at all — upfront plans provide no real benefit
It guarantees the plan will never need to change
It eliminates the need for any tool calls whatsoever
It coordinates sub-tasks whose relative order matters, and gives replanning something concrete to revise against
questions.explain: Some goals need steps in a sensible order the model can't infer one action at a time, and 'replanning' only means something if a visible plan existed to begin with.

questions.q: In the regional sales example, what happened when step 3 of the plan hit an error (a renamed region)?
options: The entire plan was discarded and the agent started over from scratch
The agent gave up and reported failure to the user immediately
Only step 3 was replaced with a corrected version; steps 1, 2, and 4 remained unaffected
Steps 1 and 2 had to be re-executed even though they had already succeeded
questions.explain: The plan's structure survived — a wrong turn corrected locally by replacing just the invalidated step, not by restarting the whole task.

questions.q: What kind of task does this lesson say actually benefits from a planning agent's upfront decomposition?
options: A task that is really just deciding a single next action, repeated — for which the plain reactive loop is simpler and just as effective
A task with several sub-tasks whose relative order matters, especially where some can run independently of others
A task that never involves any tool calls at all
Any task whatsoever, with no exceptions
questions.explain: Planning earns its keep when there's real coordination to get right — order-dependent or partially independent sub-tasks — not as a blanket upgrade for every task.

questions.q: What real cost does planning add on top of what Lesson 5 already identified for agent loops in general?
options: No additional cost of any kind — planning is always free
Planning removes all token costs from every subsequent step
Planning makes every tool call guaranteed to succeed with zero errors
The latency of the planning step itself, on top of the per-iteration costs an agent loop already carries
questions.explain: Generating the plan upfront is itself an extra model call with its own latency, stacked on top of the loop costs (latency, tokens, failure surface) Lesson 5 already covered.
